Analog Finder

Pick a Moon or Mars landing site. Every candidate place on Earth is scored on how closely it matches that site's conditions, so you can find new places to test equipment and rehearse missions.

Main finding: the closest Earth matches we found to Jezero Crater are two plateaus never proposed for Jezero, not the famous analogs: Aksai Chin, between the Karakoram and Kunlun ranges and the limestone plateau east of Kharga Oasis, Egypt, tied at 75%, both above the White Desert (72%) and Haughton Crater (68%). NASA EMIT finds carbonate at both, uniform at Kharga and patchy at Aksai Chin; Kharga is 4 h from a city, while Aksai Chin sits at 4,900 m in a remote, disputed border area.
Permanent Moon base: the best new analogs are Harrat Khaybar, Saudi Arabia for a lava-tube shelter (76%, #1 of 59 sites) and the eastern Karakoram for south-pole terrain (best match outside Antarctica).

What we found

The results behind the map: new analogs for the Moon and Mars, how we checked them, and where the method stops. Every number here can be reproduced in the map above by picking the target.

Discovery 1 · Mars · Jezero Crater

Egypt’s Western Desert limestone plateaus are among the world’s best matches to Jezero

Earth Engine scan of Egypt at 1 km against Jezero. Orange = closer match. The Nile Valley and coast stay dark: too wet and too green.

150areas in Egypt’s top 0.5%, about 5,400 km²
75%Kharga plateau at its best spot: tied for #1 of 59 sites worldwide with Aksai Chin
99–100%calcite in NASA EMIT data at 5 of 6 candidates

The scan wasn’t told where limestone is; it found carbonate terrain from satellite data alone, which matters because Jezero’s lake deposits are rich in carbonates. EMIT then corrected one guess: the area east of Lake Nasser is clay, not carbonate, so it fits Gale Crater instead (67%). The Kharga plateau is about 4 h from a city and not in a protected area: a realistic first field site.

Prior work: NASA-funded studies in the 1980s (Farouk El-Baz and colleagues) used the Kharga region’s wind-carved landforms and dunes as Mars comparisons. We found no study proposing the carbonate plateau east of Kharga as an analog for Jezero’s carbonates: that link is new here.

Discovery 2 · Moon · Mare Tranquillitatis pit

Harrat Khaybar, Saudi Arabia, matches the lunar lava-tube pit

World scan at 5 km. Green = top 0.5% of land for the pit’s surface conditions.

76%#1 of 59 sites, just ahead of Jordan’s Jawa lava tubes (76%) and Craters of the Moon, Idaho (75%)
86%of 2,000 re-weightings put Khaybar #1; always top 3
1,481 mUmm Jirsan lava tube, the longest reported in Arabia

A young basalt field with almost no vegetation, and lava tubes big enough to test shelters in. Not in a protected area; about 11 h from the nearest city. It is also #2 for Mare Imbrium (70%, after Libya’s Al Haruj) and level with Craters of the Moon for the Arsia Mons cave pits on Mars (73%): one place to rehearse lava-tube bases for both worlds.

World scans · 5 km · then measured like every other site

Searching the whole planet: 19 more candidates

Jezero. Top 0.5% of land (green) falls in Aksai Chin and the western Tibetan Plateau, the Atacama and Peruvian coast, and the Egyptian and Libyan Sahara.

Arcadia Planitia (Mars base ice). Antarctica’s ice sheet scores highest overall; outside it, the best areas are the Tibetan Plateau and the Canadian Arctic.

We took the best new area per region from the Jezero, Arcadia, lunar-pit and lunar-pole scans (19 in all), measured each one in Earth Engine over a 10 km circle exactly like our other sites, added ESA permafrost, and scored them against all nine targets.

Rock type for these 19 comes from ASTER emissivity with the same rule as the scan; we then checked 13 of them with NASA EMIT (the other 6 are polar or glaciated, outside EMIT’s view). EMIT confirmed carbonate at Aksai Chin, east of Qena and south of Al Haruj, found carbonate at 6 sites ASTER couldn’t read and clay at Moquegua, and these are now scored that way. Basalt (Al Haruj) and halite (Atacama coast) have no EMIT signature, so ASTER’s calls stand. The 6 polar and glaciated sites stay neutral.

World scan · Lunar south pole (NASA’s planned permanent base)

The best Earth matches to the lunar south pole are cold, rugged, glaciated mountains

Because the pole target is steep, frozen and icy, the world scan’s top 0.5% falls on high, glaciated mountains: the eastern Karakoram and Ladakh, Tibet’s Qiangtang plateau, Baffin Island, Siberia’s Verkhoyansk Range and Alaska’s Saint Elias Mountains. Only 2% of the top area is in Antarctica.

We measured the four biggest mountain areas as sites. Antarctica’s Dry Valleys still lead (67%), but the eastern Karakoram comes a close second (66%), top 3 in 90% of re-weightings, ahead of Allan Hills (63%) and Haughton Crater (62%). Alaska’s Saint Elias Mountains score 64% and Siberia’s Verkhoyansk Range 61%. The Karakoram site sits at 5,500 m with 19° slopes on continuous permafrost, in a remote, restricted border region about a day from the nearest city.

Settling the Jezero tie · 250 m scans

Up close, the two plateaus stay tied

We re-scanned 1° × 1° boxes around both plateaus at 250 m. At Kharga our first circle sat on the escarpment, so we measured the flat plateau 45 km south-east as a new site: 74.7% (up from 74.5%). Aksai Chin’s best scan spot scores lower once measured as a site (73.5%), so its first site stays its best (75.3%). Differences under about one point are within what the method can separate. Result: a genuine tie. Aksai Chin comes first in 52% of re-weightings, the Kharga plateau in 47%, Kharga is slightly more consistent (top 3 in 69% vs 61% of re-weightings), and NASA EMIT shows why it is the safer pick: its carbonate is uniform (100% of detections at the new best spot, 99–100% at 5 other plateau sites), while Aksai Chin’s is patchy (56% at the first site, only 11% at the 250 m best spot). A 0.6-point gap is within what the method can resolve.

Seen from orbit · ESA Sentinel-2 true colour (2024)

What the two top candidates actually look like

Plateau east of Kharga. The circle straddles the escarpment: gullied slopes on its west side, flat pale limestone plateau to the east. The oasis farms (dark patches, far left) lie outside it. No roads, fields or buildings inside.

Harrat Khaybar. Our first circle (orange) sat on the lava field’s southern edge, half on a sandy basin. After this check we moved the site 22 km north onto the basalt (green) and re-measured it in Earth Engine: its match rose from 75% to 76% and it is now #1 for the lunar pit outright.

Orange ring = the 10 km circle our Earth Engine values average over. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2024), processed in Google Earth Engine.

Caves · scan + catalog cross-check

The scan finds the surface; cave catalogs decide where tubes actually exist

Lava tubes are 10–50 m wide, far below a 5 km scan pixel, so no satellite layer can find them. We checked each scan hot spot and each volcanic site against published cave records.

Result: we added five documented lava-tube fields, including NASA’s own cave analogs, to test the ranking. Arabia’s desert lava fields come out on top: Harrat Khaybar and Jordan’s Black Desert near Jawa beat Lava Beds and El Malpais, which are greener and wetter at the surface than the Moon. Surface match plus confirmed tubes is what makes Khaybar the pick.

Does the method work?

It rediscovers the famous analogs, and the ranking holds

Limits
  • World scans run at 1–5 km: caves and small craters come from catalogs, not the scan.
  • NASA EMIT covers dry regions within ±54° latitude only; ground ice in the world scan is a temperature proxy (sites use ESA’s permafrost map).
  • Mars temperatures, Moon night temperatures and ice come from published results; slope, iron, hydrogen, elevation, Moon daytime and polar temperatures and rock cover were measured by us.
  • Scores are relative, not probabilities: sites within about one point of each other are ties, so headline numbers are rounded to whole percent.
  • Crew and operations: travel time and protected status are shown for every site, but isolation, communications, dust and regolith behaviour are not scored yet; they are the next layer, alongside a field visit.
  • Resources: we show what each site lets a team practise (ice, hydrated minerals, basalt, salts), but don’t score mineral resources yet.
  • Each site is a 10 km circle, so it can mix terrain. We checked the top two candidates in Sentinel-2 and moved Harrat Khaybar onto its lava field; other sites were not re-checked one by one.
  • Polar day and night and the low sun of the lunar south pole are shown for each site (“Sun and light”) but not scored.
  • No field visit yet: these are strong candidates, not proven analogs. Weights are judgement calls, tested with 2,000 re-weightings.

How the score works

Each place is described by ten factors, each turned into a 0–1 value: how dry it is, how bare, how cold, how big the day–night temperature swing is, how high it is (thinner air, stronger UV), how rugged, what rock it is made of, and whether it has ground ice, caves or impact craters.

Each target site has an ideal value and a weight for each factor. A site's match on one factor is 1 − |site − ideal|; rock type uses a similarity table instead (a site's secondary rock type counts at 80%). The overall match is the weighted average. New-analog potential is match × (0.7 + 0.3 × novelty), where novelty is 0.15 for known analogs, 0.5 for studied sites and 1 for new candidates.

Target fingerprints combine our own measurements (slope from LRO LOLA via LROC QuickMap and from MGS MOLA in Google Colab; Lunar Prospector iron and hydrogen; Diviner daytime and polar temperatures and rock cover) with published results (Diviner night temperatures, MEDA, THEMIS, SHARAD/SWIM, CRISM), shown under each target. Where the Moon or Mars is beyond anything on Earth (300 K day–night swings, no or very thin air, mean temperatures far below zero), the ideal is set to the Earth extreme, 1.

Getting there (travel time to the nearest city, from Weiss et al. 2018, and protected-area status from the World Database on Protected Areas) and NASA SMAP soil moisture are shown as practical information. They don't change the match score.

Data status. Earth site values are computed in Google Earth Engine over a 10 km radius (2015–2025); a site panel marks any value still taken from published descriptions. Moon and Mars slope, iron and hydrogen were measured by the team; temperatures and ice come from published results. This is a screening tool: candidates still need a field check.
